name: INA333AIDGKR
title: Micro-power, zero-drift, rail-to-rail-output instrumentation amplifier
summary: The INA333 is a three-amplifier instrumentation amplifier with an auto-zeroed core, drawing 50 µA from a 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply. One external resistor sets the gain from 1 to 1000 by G = 1 + 100 kΩ / RG. Offset is 25 µV max and drift 0.1 µV/°C at G ≥ 100, the output swings to within 50 mV of each rail, and the inputs carry RFI filters. It comes in an 8-pin VSSOP and an 8-pin WSON, specified from -40 °C to 125 °C.

circuits.title: Low-power log function circuit for portable battery-powered systems (example glucose meter)
circuits.description: Two OPA369 transdiode stages, each with a diode-connected NPN of a matched dual pair from its inverting input to its output. One stage takes the 10 nA input current, the other a reference current set by a 2.5 V source across a 2.5 MΩ resistor. The INA333, gain set by 14 kΩ, takes the difference of the two stage outputs; its REF sits at the 2.5 V Vref+ rail. An R8 10 kΩ, C1 1 nF filter follows, and an OPA335 follower buffers it for a sampling converter of 33 kHz or more. The logging transistors have no temperature compensation in this circuit.

circuits.title: Four-wire, 3 V conditioner for a PT100 RTD with programmable-gain acquisition
circuits.description: A Pt100 is fed from 3 V through R1 (2 kΩ) and returned to ground through a current sink (BF256A JFET, OPA333, 2.5 kΩ, referenced to VREF from a REF3212). Its two sense leads go to the INA333: the RTD- lead directly to VIN-, the RTD+ lead through an OPA333 follower and RZERO (100 Ω) to VIN+. A second sink of the same form (BF256A, OPA333, 2.5 kΩ, VREF) draws current through RZERO. RGAIN of 100 kΩ sets G = 2; REF goes to VREF+. VDIFF goes on to a PGA112 and an MSP430. RWa to RWd (3, 3, 4, 3 Ω) stand for lead resistance and show that the four-wire scheme ignores lead mismatch.

equations.name: Total offset referred to the input

operation.text: A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier on one die, built on the zero-drift OPA333 amplifier core. Input amplifiers A1 and A2 each have a 50 kΩ feedback resistor ending at an RG pin; A3, a difference stage with four 150 kΩ resistors, takes their outputs and refers the result to REF. Both inputs pass through RFI filters. Laser trimming of the internal resistors gives the high CMRR and the small gain error.

The internal amplifiers auto-calibrate: a 350 kHz continuous-time amplifier stays in the signal path and its offset is corrected every 8 µs. About 100 µs after power is applied the offset reaches its specified accuracy. The scheme produces no aliasing and no flicker (1/f) noise.

One resistor between pins 1 and 8 sets the gain. The 100 kΩ in the gain equation is A1's and A2's feedback resistors in series; their accuracy and temperature coefficient are inside the gain-error and gain-drift figures, while the external RG adds its own tolerance and drift. At high gain RG is small, so wiring resistance counts, and a socket adds gain error, possibly unstable, at gains near 100 and above. Stray capacitance above a few pF on pins 1 and 8 can cause instability; equal parasitics on the two RG pins keep CMRR flat with frequency.

The output is measured from REF, usually grounded. REF must see a low impedance to keep common-mode rejection: up to 15 Ω of series resistance still meets the CMRR figure, but a few tens of ohms degrade it noticeably. A voltage on REF adds to the output, so an op-amp follower driving REF can trim the output offset or shift the output level.

Input impedance is about 100 GΩ and bias current typically ±70 pA, changing little with input voltage. Each input still needs a DC path to ground for its bias current; without one the inputs drift outside the common-mode range and the input amplifiers saturate. With a low differential source resistance one resistor on one input is enough (thermocouple). With a higher source impedance, a matched pair of resistors, one per input, keeps the input balanced; that lowers the offset caused by bias current and improves rejection of fast common-mode signals.

The input stage is linear from about 0.1 V above V– to 0.1 V below V+. As the differential input drives the output away from REF, the swing limits of A1 and A2 narrow that range, so the usable common-mode range depends on output voltage and supply. An overload can look like a normal output: if both input amplifiers are driven to their positive limit, A3 sees almost no difference and the output sits near 0 V.

1.8 V to 5.5 V single, or ±0.9 V to ±2.75 V split. More than 7 V can destroy the part. Best performance is with 3.3 V to 5 V. Decoupling where the supply enters the circuit makes up for trace and source impedance; a 0.1 µF capacitor goes close across the supply pins. Most parameters change only a little down to ±0.9 V, but at low supply the input voltages need care to stay in the linear range.

On one supply REF is usually tied to mid-supply, so zero differential input gives a mid-supply output. With the load returned to ground the output gets to within about 50 mV of ground; the swing narrows as output current rises. Both inputs must stay at least 0.1 V above ground for linear operation, so the inverting input cannot simply be grounded to measure a signal on the non-inverting input.

Internal diodes clamp each input to the supply rails. If an input can go more than 0.3 V past a rail, keep its current below 10 mA, normally with a series resistor; a source that limits its own current needs none.

Each input, VIN+ and VIN–, has an on-chip RC low-pass with its corner at 8 MHz, reducing offset shifts caused by radio-frequency interference. Strong RF fields can still shift the offset and may need shielding.
Because of the auto-calibration, low-frequency noise stays flat: typically 50 nV/√Hz at G = 100, and about 1 µVPP from 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz at G = 100.

Short traces, a ground plane, and surface-mount parts close to the pins. The gain resistor sits beside pins 1 and 8; bypass capacitors go from V+ and from V– to ground next to the pins. The WSON exposed pad is soldered to a board pad.
ESD protection is limited; the MOS gates are at risk. Store and handle with the leads shorted together or in conductive foam.
An automotive-qualified version is sold as INA333-Q1.
